newsitem.title: USA: Top official says CIA chief needs set term.
newsitem.headline: Top official says CIA chief needs set term.

text.p: The Central Intelligence Agency official in charge of investigating the agency's problems called on Tuesday for a statutory six- or seven-year term for the top U.S. spymaster.

In unusually candid remarks, CIA inspector general Frederick Hitz also said the agency's officer corps needed upgrading and must recapture its sense of mission. In addition, he acknowledged structural impediments to CIA declassification of Cold War secrets.
Referring to a "substantial erosion in public support for U.S. intelligence agencies," Hitz said the United States must not let past intelligence embarrassments become "a metaphor for CIA."

"The U.S. needs a first-rate intelligence agency operating with a high degree of professional competence and with solid morale or we will not meet the challenges of the 21st century," he told a luncheon.

Hitz suggested that still more counter-spy measures may be needed to protect national security secrets, citing the cases of Aldrich Ames, a 31-year veteran CIA official who confessed in April 1994 to spying for Moscow for nine years, and Harold Nicholson, an ex-CIA station chief awaiting trial on charges of spying for Moscow.
"The occurrence of Nicholson after the Ames case has probably convinced any person who thinks it's only going to happen once in a generation that that's not so," he said.
"What in the world caused him to think when Ames was busting out all over in 1994 that he could pull this little prank off?" Hitz went on.

Hitz, the CIA's in-house watchdog since 1990, cited as an example of a too frequent rotation President Bill Clinton's decision last week to replace CIA Director John Deutch with Anthony Lake, his current national security adviser, as part of a revamped second-term administration.
Lake would be Clinton's third director of central intelligence and the agency's fifth in just over five years.

Since 1991, the CIA and its companion spy outfits have been led by William Webster, who resigned; Robert Gates, who served 14 months before a newly elected Clinton replaced him; James Woolsey, who lasted 23 months before he was squeezed out, and Deutch, who has presided for the past 20 months.
"CIA needs stability and consistency in its leadership," Hitz said. "This is too much change at the top."

He said he had concluded that the director of central intelligence, who runs the CIA and serves as board chairman of the 12 other U.S. spy outfits, should serve a six- or seven-year term to provide management continuity along the lines of the director of the Federal Bureau of Investigation and chairman of the joint chiefs of staff, each of whom has a statutory term.
Hitz said the CIA had many "pockets of exceptional ability and performance. But there are inconsistencies and gaps in our coverage and performance that we must concentrate on trying to improve."

Replying to a question, Hitz disclosed that he had reported to the "front office" on reasons for the failure to meet declassification goals on Cold War covert actions. He blamed it on division of responsiblity among three CIA offices. His recommended solution, he said, was simple: "Put somebody in charge. Give him the resources. Give him a boot in the fanny and get him cracking."
